questions.stem: Which form completes „Sie ___ ihre Tasche daheim vergessen.“ ('She had forgotten her bag at home')?
questions.explanation: The pluperfect is the imperfect of the auxiliary plus the participle, and „vergessen“ takes „haben“: „sie hatte … vergessen“. „Hat“ would make the perfect, 'she has forgotten'.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Als wir am Bahnhof ankamen, ___ der Zug schon abgefahren.“?
questions.explanation: The train left before they arrived, so the pluperfect, and „abfahren“ is a verb of movement that takes „sein“: „war … abgefahren“. „Hatte“ picks the wrong auxiliary; „ist“ is the right auxiliary in the wrong tense.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Du ___ in Wien viel sehen.“ ('You will see a lot in Vienna')?
questions.explanation: The future is „werden“ plus an infinitive, and the du-form is „wirst“. „Willst“ is from „wollen“, 'to want', the false friend of English 'will'.

questions.stem: What does „Morgen geht er wieder zur Arbeit“ mean?
options: He wants to go back to work tomorrow
He is going back to work tomorrow
He went back to work this morning
He goes to work every morning
questions.explanation: German often uses the present with a time word for the future, so „morgen geht er“ is 'tomorrow he goes'. 'Every morning' would be „morgens“ or „jeden Morgen“.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of „bringen“?
questions.explanation: „Bringen“ is a mixed verb: the vowel changes like a strong verb, but it ends in -t like a weak one, as in „denken – gedacht“. „Gebrungen“ copies the pattern of „singen – gesungen“, which this verb does not follow.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich ___ nicht, dass du heute kommst.“ ('I didn't know you were coming today')?
questions.explanation: „Wissen“ is a mixed verb with the imperfect „wusste“. „Wüsste“ is Subjunctive 2, 'would know', which does not fit a plain statement about the past.

questions.stem: Which verb takes „sein“ in the perfect tense?
questions.explanation: „Passieren“, like „geschehen“, takes „sein“: „es ist passiert“. The others take a direct object and „haben“: „ich habe ihn besucht“, „wir haben den Tag verbracht“.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses „mitnehmen“ correctly in the present tense?
questions.explanation: In a main clause the separable prefix goes to the end, with the verb second: „wir nehmen … mit“. The prefix stays attached only when the verb itself goes last, as in a dass-clause.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of „bekommen“?
questions.explanation: Verbs with an inseparable prefix (be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer-) add no ge-: „ich habe gute Noten bekommen“. „Gekommen“ belongs to „kommen“, a different verb.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich weiß nicht, wann der Zug ___.“ (ankommen)?
questions.explanation: „Wann“ introduces an indirect question, which sends the verb to the end, and there the separable verb joins up again: „wann der Zug ankommt“. „Kommt an“ is the main-clause order.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Im Winter ist es schwer, früh ___.“ (aufstehen)?
questions.explanation: With a separable verb, „zu“ goes between the prefix and the stem and the whole is written as one word: „aufzustehen“, „mitzukommen“. With an ordinary verb it stands alone: „zu lesen“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Die Kinder ___ sich auf die Ferien.“ ('The children were looking forward to the holidays')?
questions.explanation: 'Were looking forward' is the imperfect, and „freuen“ is weak, so -te plus the plural ending: „sie freuten sich“. „Freute“ is the singular form.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich ___ mich gestern erkältet.“ ('I caught a cold yesterday')?
questions.explanation: Reflexive verbs always take „haben“ in the perfect: „ich habe mich erkältet“. „Bin“ is a guess from the idea of a change of state, but the reflexive pronoun makes it a haben-verb.

questions.stem: Which modal verb expresses permission?
questions.explanation: „Dürfen“ is 'to be allowed to': „Darf ich hier parken?“ „Sollen“ is what you are supposed to do, and „mögen“ is liking.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Du ___ nicht so laut sprechen – das Baby schläft.“ ('You mustn't')?
questions.explanation: 'Mustn't' forbids, and German forbids with „nicht dürfen“. „Du musst nicht“ means 'you don't have to', a false friend that reverses the meaning.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich habe gestern bis zehn Uhr arbeiten ___.“?
questions.explanation: A modal with another infinitive forms its perfect with two infinitives, the double infinitive: „ich habe arbeiten müssen“. „Gemusst“ is used only when the modal stands alone: „Ich habe es gemusst“.

questions.stem: What is the du-imperative of „lesen“ in standard German?
questions.explanation: Verbs that change e to i or ie in the du-form keep that change in the imperative and drop the ending: „du liest“ → „Lies!“, „du gibst“ → „Gib!“. „Lese!“ ignores the vowel change.

questions.stem: How do you politely tell an adult stranger 'Please sit down'?
questions.explanation: The Sie-imperative puts the verb first, then „Sie“, then the reflexive „sich“. „Setzen Sie bitte“ drops the reflexive pronoun, which „sich setzen“ cannot do without.

questions.stem: Which form completes „___ ich bitte etwas bestellen?“ ('Could I order something, please?')?
questions.explanation: „Könnte“, the Subjunctive 2 of „können“, makes a polite request. Without the umlaut, „konnte“ is the imperfect, 'could' in the sense of 'was able to'.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Wenn sie mehr Zeit ___, würden sie hier bleiben.“?
questions.explanation: An unreal condition uses Subjunctive 2 on both sides: „hätten“ in the wenn-clause and „würden … bleiben“ in the main clause. „Hatten“ without the umlaut is the plain imperfect.

questions.stem: Which sentence imagines something that is not true now?
options: Als ich reich war, reiste ich.
Wenn ich reich wäre, würde ich reisen.
Wenn ich reich war, reiste ich.
Wenn ich reich bin, reise ich.
questions.explanation: „Wäre … würde“ is Subjunctive 2, an unreal present condition: 'if I were rich, I would travel'. „Wenn ich reich bin“ is a real possibility, and the two past forms describe what actually happened.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Du ___ wirklich mehr schlafen.“ ('You really ought to sleep more')?
questions.explanation: Advice uses „sollte“, the Subjunctive 2 of „sollen“. „Musstest“ is the imperfect of „müssen“, 'you had to', which reports a past obligation rather than giving advice.

questions.stem: What does „Mehrere Filme wurden darüber gedreht“ mean?
options: Several films were made about it
Several films are being made about it
Several films will be made about it
Several films had made it famous
questions.explanation: „Wurden“ plus a participle is the imperfect passive, 'were made'. The present passive would be „werden … gedreht“, and the future „werden … gedreht werden“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Das alte Haus ___ zurzeit renoviert.“ ('is being renovated at the moment')?
questions.explanation: The present passive is „werden“ plus the participle: „das Haus wird renoviert“. „Ist renoviert“ describes the finished state, 'is renovated', not the work in progress.

questions.stem: Which words complete „Der Tisch muss noch ___.“ ('The table still has to be cleared')?
questions.explanation: A passive after a modal is participle plus „werden“ at the end: „muss abgeräumt werden“. „Worden“ belongs only in the perfect passive, after „sein“.

questions.stem: What does „Ihm wird viel geholfen“ mean?
options: He will help a great deal
He is given a lot of help
He helps a lot of people
questions.explanation: „Helfen“ takes the dative, and the dative object stays dative in the passive, so the sentence has no subject: 'to him a lot of help is given'. „Er wird helfen“ would be the future, 'he will help'.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Das Rathaus ist im Jahr 1905 gebaut ___.“?
questions.explanation: The perfect passive is „sein“ plus the participle plus „worden“. „Geworden“ is the participle of „werden“ as 'become': „er ist Arzt geworden“.

questions.stem: What does „Es ist schade, dass du nicht kommen kannst“ mean?
options: It's lucky that you can't come
It's obvious that you can't come
It's a pity that you can't come
It's harmful that you can't come
questions.explanation: „Es ist schade“ is 'it's a pity'. It is easy to confuse with „schädlich“, 'harmful', because the two words look alike.

questions.stem: What does „Das stimmt“ mean in a conversation?
questions.explanation: „Es stimmt“ or „das stimmt“ agrees that something is correct. 'That's enough' is „das reicht“, and 'that's a pity' is „das ist schade“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Er sah den Zug ___.“ ('He saw the train coming')?
questions.explanation: Verbs of perception such as „sehen“ and „hören“ take a plain infinitive with no „zu“: „er sah den Zug kommen“. English uses '-ing' here, which tempts students towards a participle.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Er hat sich die Haare schneiden ___.“ ('He had his hair cut')?
questions.explanation: „Lassen“ with another infinitive forms its perfect with a double infinitive, like a modal: „hat … schneiden lassen“. It means having something done by someone else.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Interessieren Sie sich ___ das neue Angebot?“?
questions.explanation: The verb is „sich interessieren für“. The noun takes a different preposition, „das Interesse an“, which is why „an“ is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Die Gasemissionen schaden ___ Umwelt.“?
questions.explanation: „Schaden“ takes a dative object, and „Umwelt“ is feminine, so „der Umwelt“. „Die Umwelt“ treats it as a direct object, as English 'harm the environment' does.

questions.stem: Which sentence follows the time–manner–place order?
options: Wir fahren jedes Jahr nach Wien mit dem Zug.
Wir fahren jedes Jahr mit dem Zug nach Wien.
Wir fahren mit dem Zug jedes Jahr nach Wien.
Wir fahren nach Wien jedes Jahr mit dem Zug.
questions.explanation: After the verb, German puts when (jedes Jahr), then how (mit dem Zug), then where (nach Wien). English tends to put place before time, which is the order to unlearn.

questions.stem: Which sentence simply says the purchase did not happen?
options: Wir haben das Auto nicht gekauft.
Wir haben nicht das Auto gekauft.
Wir nicht haben das Auto gekauft.
Wir haben das Auto gekauft nicht.
questions.explanation: To negate the whole statement, „nicht“ goes after the object and before the participle. „Nicht das Auto“ negates only the car, implying they bought something else.

questions.stem: Which ending is correct in written German: „Ich lerne Deutsch, weil …“?
questions.explanation: „Weil“ is subordinating, so the conjugated verb goes to the very end, after the infinitive. Main-clause order after „weil“ is heard in casual speech but is not written German.

questions.stem: Which words complete „Wenn er ankommt, ___.“ ('he should call us')?
questions.explanation: A subordinate clause at the start fills the first position, so the main clause begins with its verb: „…, soll er uns anrufen“. Starting with „er“ puts the verb third.

questions.stem: In written German, which word completes „Ich komme heute nicht mit, ___ ich habe keine Zeit.“?
questions.explanation: The clause keeps main-clause order („ich habe“), so it needs a coordinating conjunction, and the one meaning 'because' is „denn“. „Weil“ would send „habe“ to the end.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Er fährt nicht mit dem Bus, ___ mit dem Rad.“?
questions.explanation: After a negative, „sondern“ gives the correct alternative: 'not … but rather'. „Aber“ adds a contrast without replacing the first idea.

questions.stem: Which pair completes „Ich spreche ___ Deutsch ___ Französisch.“ ('both … and')?
questions.explanation: „Sowohl … als auch“ is 'both … and'. „Weder … noch“ is 'neither … nor' and „entweder … oder“ is 'either … or', which is a choice rather than both.

questions.stem: Which words complete „Ich möchte gern wissen, ___.“ ('what his name is')?
questions.explanation: An indirect question is a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end: „wie er heißt“. German asks a name with „wie“, not „was“.

questions.stem: Which pair completes „Sie fährt nur mit dem Rad, ___ die Umwelt ___ schützen.“?
questions.explanation: Purpose with an infinitive is „um … zu“, with the infinitive last. „Damit“ also expresses purpose but introduces a clause with its own subject and verb, never „zu“.

questions.stem: Which words complete „Habt ihr Lust, mit uns ___?“ ('Do you feel like coming with us?')?
questions.explanation: „Lust haben“ is followed by an infinitive clause with „zu“, and „zu“ plus the infinitive goes last. Modals, „lassen“ and verbs of perception and motion take a bare infinitive, but „Lust haben“ does not.

questions.stem: Which word completes „___ ich zehn Jahre alt war, zogen wir nach Melbourne.“?
questions.explanation: „Als“ is for a single event or period in the past. „Wenn“ is for repeated past events or the present and future, and „wann“ asks a question about time.

questions.stem: Which word completes „___ es stark regnete, sind wir spazieren gegangen.“?
questions.explanation: „Obwohl“, 'although', introduces a clause with the verb at the end, as „regnete“ is here. „Trotzdem“ means 'nevertheless' but is an adverb, and „denn“ only links two main clauses and never comes first, so neither can introduce this clause.
